title: Mental Models and Professional Development
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: Adam Kohlbeck uses a new preprint literature review by Dutch researcher Annemarieke Schepers, covering 22 studies of secondary teachers' mental models, as a lens on instructional coaching and professional learning. The review finds little coherence in how professional development surfaces, changes and supports teachers' mental models, and suggests treating those three elements as a responsive design rather than a fixed procedure. Kohlbeck draws out two claims: that mental models shape how teachers interpret and regulate classroom situations, and that those models are built from beliefs and assumptions as well as knowledge. The central move is to argue that most professional learning works only on the knowledge component, because knowledge is easier to check, teach and update across a group, while beliefs are more varied, more personal and more tightly held. Worked vignettes (a Year 9 English teacher supplying the word 'guilt' mid-discussion, and a coached teacher named Liam whose walk toward a cold-called student was driven by a belief that all students should feel valued) show how interpretation and values drive in-the-moment decisions. For coaches, the practical upshot is to shift questioning from judging outcomes toward surfacing goals and the reasoning behind actions, so beliefs can be examined rather than overridden.
points: Schepers' review of 22 studies finds no coherent account of how to surface, change and support teachers' mental models, so Kohlbeck recommends treating PD as responsive design rather than a neat three-step procedure.
Mental models bring structure to the ill-structured classroom: teachers match salient cues to prior experience and then regulate the situation, as in the Romeo and Tybalt turn-and-talk example.

Most professional learning targets knowledge (for example cognitive load theory) because it is easy to check and fill gaps, while beliefs and assumptions go largely unexamined despite shaping classroom decisions.
Coaches should replace 'How do you think it went?' with questions about the teacher's goal and what drove a given action, which surfaces the model before trying to develop it.
The Liam cold-calling case shows that correcting a move without addressing the underlying value (making students feel valued) is unlikely to stick when the next similar situation arises.
quotes: The paper finds that there is a relative lack of coherence about how best to surface, change and support teachers’ mental models. This means that while we have methods that help us to do these three elements, we don’t yet understand how they interact together especially well.

I find this so interesting because it reminds us that mental models help to bring structure to what is naturally an ill-structured system. Where the lack of structure in the system means that so much is dependent on how situations are interpreted and how teachers act on that interpretation, it makes a strong case for mental models being central to how we understand the effectiveness of teaching.

I think that it is far less common for professional learning to consider assumptions and beliefs that teachers bring to situations. So, if we accept that mental models lead to the decisions we make in the classroom and therefore they tell us a lot about teaching quality, we are potentially missing a trick if we don’t deliberately surface, examine and develop assumptions and beliefs.

I can’t have the same success rate with changing beliefs and assumptions, partly because they tend to be more varied within a group than knowledge and partly because people tend to hold onto beliefs and assumptions more tightly than knowledge – they feel more personal. It is also much more difficult to surface assumptions and beliefs than knowledge.

Of course, in the busy and fast paced reality of school life, it is easy to slip into focusing on the actions and allowing our feedback to focus on the correction of teaching moves rather than on the making of meaning that drove the decision to use that teaching move.
If we want to develop mental models, we first need to surface them and this shift in questioning approach can really help us to do that.

Beliefs are particularly important to teachers because, like many vocational professions, there is a moral drive behind many peoples’ decision to enter it. This means that our idea of what good practice is, is often shaped by what we believe about education and linked to that, what we value most about it.

If I had focused on his knowledge, I might have improved what he knows but the chances of him letting this knowledge override his natural beliefs and values in the next similar situation he had found himself in, would be slim.
